headline: Michigan Defies Trump’s Vaccine Order While Drugmakers Reject Split MMR Shot
deck: The state’s refusal to rewrite its vaccine rules exposes a widening rift over a former president’s divisive plan to separate the measles-mumps-rubella inoculation.
body: Michigan is standing firm on its child vaccination policies, explicitly rejecting a 2024 executive order from former President Donald Trump that sought to split the combined MMR vaccine into separate shots. State health officials confirmed Friday they will not alter existing mandates, which require schoolchildren to receive the two-dose MMR immunization. The decision arrives less than 90 days before Michigan’s next legislative session, where lawmakers are expected to introduce bills codifying the current rules. Public health advocates called the move a critical safeguard against outbreaks of measles, a disease declared eliminated in the U.S. in 2000 but resurgent in pockets with low vaccination rates.

Trump’s order targeted the MMR vaccine specifically, proposing its component vaccines be administered separately despite decades of clinical consensus favoring the combined shot. The directive cited concerns about potential side effects, though no new safety data supported the change. Medical experts immediately criticized the proposal as scientifically baseless and logistically chaotic, noting that splitting the vaccine would require additional doctor visits and increase the risk of children not completing the full immunization series. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has repeatedly affirmed the safety and efficacy of the combined MMR vaccine, which has been in use since 1971.

Drug manufacturers have signaled outright disinterest in complying with the order, according to industry sources cited by The Hill. Two of the three companies that produce MMR vaccines in the U.S. told federal regulators they would not retool production lines to create standalone formulations. ‘The economics don’t work,’ said one executive, who spoke on condition of anonymity. ‘The volumes aren’t there for a split vaccine, and the liability risks outweigh any potential benefit.’ The third manufacturer, Merck, declined to comment on whether it would consider modifying its manufacturing process.

Voter sentiment appears firmly against the executive order, according to a national poll conducted last month by the Kaiser Family Foundation. Only 22% of respondents supported splitting the MMR vaccine, while 68% opposed the idea—including 54% of respondents who identified as Republicans. The poll’s margin of error was 3 percentage points. Public health researchers say the results reflect growing fatigue with politicized health mandates, particularly among suburban parents who have borne the brunt of school vaccine debates in recent years.

The backlash extends beyond Michigan. In an op-ed for The Washington Post, Dr. Paul Offit, a vaccine developer and director of the Vaccine Education Center at Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, called Trump’s order ‘a dangerous distraction from real threats to public health.’ Offit wrote, ‘This idea makes me sick—not because the MMR vaccine is unsafe, but because it diverts attention from the real work of improving vaccination rates. Splitting the vaccine won’t make kids safer; it will make them sicker.’

The Guardian’s editorial board took an even sharper tone, accusing the executive order of ‘endangering the children he claims to care about.’ The newspaper argued that Trump’s proposal was rooted in conspiracy theories about vaccine safety, pointing to the former president’s repeated amplification of debunked claims linking vaccines to autism. ‘If Donald Trump truly wanted to protect children,’ the editorial read, ‘he would stop undermining the very systems designed to keep them healthy.’

Michigan’s stance highlights a broader tension between state autonomy and federal directives in public health—a debate that flared during the COVID-19 pandemic and now threatens to reignite over childhood vaccines. State Senator Sarah Anthony, a Democrat from Lansing, said the legislature would introduce a bill next session to explicitly ban any future attempts to split the MMR vaccine. ‘We’re not going to let politics dictate what’s medically sound,’ Anthony told reporters. ‘Our kids deserve better than ideological games with their health.’

The standoff raises questions about the enforceability of Trump’s executive order, which lacks funding or penalties for noncompliance. Health policy experts note that without buy-in from states, drugmakers, or the CDC, the directive may remain unenforceable—a fate shared by many of Trump’s other public health initiatives. ‘An executive order without teeth is just a suggestion,’ said Dr. Peter Hotez, a vaccine scientist at Baylor College of Medicine. ‘And in this case, it’s a dangerous one.’
